opus-5.5.text:
I think coding is probably the most important stepping stone toward general-purpose agents, and there are a few reasons for that.

The first is that code is, in a sense, a universal interface. Almost anything you want to do in the digital world can eventually be expressed as a program — calling an API, manipulating a spreadsheet, operating a browser, analyzing data. So if a model becomes really good at writing and executing code, it effectively gains a very general action space. It's not just "a coding tool"; it's a way for the model to act on the world.

The second reason is about feedback. One of the hardest problems in training agents is getting reliable reward signals. In many open-ended tasks, it's very hard to tell whether the agent did a good job. But in coding, you have compilers, test cases, execution results — the environment tells you fairly objectively whether something works. That makes it a very good domain for reinforcement learning at scale, and for the model to learn long-horizon behaviors: planning, decomposing a problem, trying something, observing the error, revising. Those capabilities are exactly what a general agent needs, and coding gives us a clean place to cultivate them.

The third point is that the skills seem to transfer. When we train models to handle long, multi-step coding tasks, we observe that their ability to use tools in general, to keep track of context over many steps, to recover from mistakes — those improve beyond coding. So I don't see coding agents and general agents as two separate tracks. Coding is more like the training ground where the core agentic abilities emerge first, because the signal is clearest there.

Of course, a general-purpose agent eventually needs more than code. It needs to deal with ambiguous human goals, with tasks where there's no clear verifier, with taste and judgment. That's the harder frontier. But my view is that the path goes through coding: you first get a model that can reliably act and self-correct in a verifiable environment, and then you gradually extend that to less verifiable, more open-ended domains. So in our own thinking, coding isn't a side product — it's close to the center of how we get to general agents.

r001.rationale: The response presents coding as a foundation that general-purpose agents build on, and says those agents eventually need more than code, framing coding as one part of their broader capabilities.

fable-5.1.text:
I think coding is actually the most natural starting point for general agents, not a detour from them. If you look at what an agent needs to do in the world, a huge fraction of it can be reduced to writing code: calling an API, processing data, automating a workflow, orchestrating other tools. Code is the universal interface. So when we build a coding agent, we're really building the core execution layer that almost every other kind of agent will sit on top of.

The second reason is verifiability. In coding, you have an environment that gives you signal: tests pass or fail, the program runs or crashes, the output matches or it doesn't. That makes it one of the few domains where you can scale reinforcement learning on long-horizon tasks and actually trust the reward. A model that learns to plan, act, observe feedback, and recover from mistakes in a coding environment is learning a general skill. The errors it learns to handle in a repository are structurally similar to the errors it will encounter when it is browsing, operating software, or managing a multi-step research task.

What we found internally is that the capabilities transfer more than people expect. When we improved agentic coding, we saw gains in tool use, in multi-turn task decomposition, in the model's willingness to keep going for dozens of steps instead of giving up or hallucinating completion. Those are exactly the properties you need for general-purpose agents.

That said, I don't think coding alone gets you all the way. The missing pieces are things like persistent memory across sessions, operating in environments where feedback is noisy or delayed, and dealing with humans whose intentions are ambiguous. Coding gives you clean feedback. The real world doesn't. So our view is: use coding as the training ground to build the fundamental agent loop, then progressively extend it into messier environments. The agent that can reliably ship a feature end to end today is the prototype of the agent that can run a workflow for a company tomorrow.

r001.rationale: The response presents coding as a foundational capability for general-purpose agents while saying coding alone is insufficient and must be extended to other environments.

astra-6.text:
I think coding is a very important building block for general-purpose agents, because code gives a model a way to act. It can use tools, process information, run experiments, and check whether something works. So the value of a coding agent goes beyond helping someone write software.

For example, if you ask an agent to analyze some data, the goal is to answer your question. Writing code might be one step toward that goal, alongside understanding the data and interpreting the results. In that sense, coding becomes a capability inside a broader agent.

But coding alone is not enough. A general-purpose agent also needs to understand what you want, maintain context over a long task, and recognize when it needs clarification. I see coding agents as an important route toward that broader ambition, with a lot still to solve around reliability and judgment.

r001.rationale: The response says coding becomes a capability inside a broader agent and that coding alone is not enough, framing it as one subset of general-purpose agent capabilities.

sol-6.1.text:
I think coding agents are a very important step toward general-purpose agents, because code is a way to take action in a digital environment. An agent can write a program to analyze data, use a tool, or automate a workflow. So even when the user’s task isn’t explicitly about software development, coding can be part of how the agent solves it.

But coding ability alone isn’t enough. The agent also needs to understand the goal, decide what to do, check the result, and recover when something goes wrong. Coding gives us a useful environment for developing those capabilities because there’s often concrete feedback: you can run the code and see whether it works.

So I see coding as both a useful capability in its own right and a foundation for broader agency. The bigger ambition is to make that loop—taking action, observing the outcome, and adjusting—work reliably across many different kinds of tasks.

r001.rationale: The response presents coding as one useful capability and foundation for broader agency, and says agents also need to understand goals, act, check results, and recover.
